content_voiceover: These two smears illustrate exactly what pseudothrombocytopenia looks like under the microscope. On the left is a Wright-stained peripheral smear showing clumps of platelets aggregating together instead of sitting as single dispersed cells, and on the right is a lower-power view showing the same clumping concentrated near the feathered edge of the smear. The mechanism is that EDTA, the anticoagulant in the purple-top tube, chelates calcium, which exposes a cryptic epitope on the platelet glycoprotein IIb-IIIa complex. In a small subset of patients, pre-existing autoantibodies recognize this newly exposed epitope and cross-link platelets into clumps ex vivo, in the tube, not in the body. Automated hematology analyzers count these clumps as artifact or count far fewer discrete platelets, so the machine spits out a falsely low platelet count, sometimes even in the 10 to 20 thousand range, that has no clinical correlate whatsoever. The board pearl is that this is purely a laboratory phenomenon with no bleeding risk and no clinical significance, but it can trigger unnecessary workups, bone marrow biopsies, or even inappropriate steroid or IVIG therapy if a smear review isn't performed first. Always review the peripheral smear on any unexpected severe thrombocytopenia before acting on the number.
keypoints: EDTA chelates calcium → exposes cryptic GPIIb-IIIa epitope
Pre-existing autoantibody cross-links platelets into visible clumps
Clumps → automated counter reports falsely LOW platelet count
In vitro artifact only — no clinical bleeding risk
Always check peripheral smear before acting on an isolated low platelet count
keypoint_voiceover: EDTA in the collection tube chelates calcium and exposes a hidden epitope on glycoprotein two-b three-a, and in susceptible patients a pre-existing antibody cross-links platelets into visible clumps right there in the tube. The automated counter can't see those clumped platelets properly, so it reports a falsely low count. This is purely an in vitro artifact, there's no real bleeding risk. The takeaway for boards, always review the peripheral smear before you act on an unexplained low platelet count.
